In all seriousness, I don't want to see any Windows apps on Linux. Software for Windows is developed differently, and the way software is handled in Windows has been creeping into Linux for years.

I choose Firefox as example. They publish a new version every six months, with new features and creep. If you want a bugfix, install the new version, which may also change the user interface, and some third-party extensions may stop working. That may be acceptable in Windows, which has no stable releases and no package management and every vendor has to develop their own software maintenance solution. It is unacceptable in any serious environment, where people need to get work done without the underlying system and tools changing without warning.

The Mozilla team of Debian works around this, by backporting bugfixes to previous versions, providing the user with a stable and secure work environment, as it should be. It shouldn't be a workaround in the first place.

Games are different. Supporting stable versions causes breakage in networked games. Whenever a server is upgraded to a never version, and the protocol changes ever so subtly, the clients need to be upgraded as well. Somehow this is not a problem with protocols for mail, web, chat, databases, what have you.

Currently, games are the only thing Windows is useable for. For work, even Microsoft Office itself introduces incompatibilities among different versions.

So I don't want to see any Windows software on Linux. Cross-platform software for Linux, BSD, and UNIX takes little effort, it is only Windows that always requires special handling. Even for web development, Microsoft requires special workarounds. I want to see Windows become compliant with the standards of the rest of the world, even if it requires a compatibility layer like the one in FreeBSD, or go the way of the Atari.
